analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and funds it with new taxes on high earners and investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee — introduced with zero cosponsors, it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits for the people who get the least from it: a higher minimum benefit for lifetime low earners, a 5% boost for beneficiaries 82 and older, cost-of-living adjustments tied to a senior-specific inflation index, retirement credit for unpaid caregivers, and an end to the five-month waiting period for disability benefits. To pay for it, the bill raises the tax on investment income from 3.8% to 6.8% and, for a transition period, applies Social Security payroll tax to wages above the annual cap. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries, weighted toward the poorest and oldest. The bill raises the minimum benefit for low lifetime earners up to a poverty-line-based floor that grows with years worked [S2], boosts benefits 5% for people 82 or older or who have drawn benefits for 20 years [S2], switches inflation adjustments to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which typically rises faster because of medical costs [S2], lets unpaid caregivers of young children or chronically dependent relatives earn retirement credit [S2], eliminates the five-month waiting period for disability benefits and the waiting period for surviving spouse benefits [S2], and prevents the higher benefits from pushing anyone off SSI, Medicaid, or CHIP [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income and long-time Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum benefit for lifetime low earners to a floor based on the federal poverty line, scaling up from 6.25% at 11 years of work to 125% of poverty at 30 or more years, so a full-career low wage worker is lifted toward the poverty line.

Adds a 5% benefit increase for long-term eligible individuals — those who have reached age 82 or drawn benefits for 240 months — targeting the oldest retirees, who have typically outlived their savings.

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which weights the medical and housing costs that dominate seniors' budgets and historically rises faster than the index now used.

Credits unpaid caregivers with deemed wages — half the national average wage, or the full average for care of a child under 6 or a chronically dependent relative — so years spent raising children or caring for sick family members no longer zero out a retirement record.

Eliminates the five-month waiting period before disability insurance benefits begin and the waiting period for surviving spouse benefits, so disabled workers and widows get paid starting the first month they qualify.
Raises the first factor in the benefit formula from 90% to 95% of average earnings, which increases benefits proportionally more for the lowest earners.
Prevents higher Social Security checks from pushing beneficiaries over income limits for SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP, so the increase reaches people instead of being clawed back.

Pays for the expansion by raising the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 6.8%, routing 44.1% of it to the Social Security trust fund, and applying Social Security payroll tax to wages above the annual cap during a 2025-2028 transition.

analysis.who_pays: High-income households. Investors would pay 3 percentage points more on investment income — the net investment income tax goes from 3.8% to 6.8% starting in 2025 [S2]. High earners and self-employed people making above the annual Social Security wage cap would pay Social Security tax on the portion of earnings above the cap during 2025 through 2028 (phased at 80%, 60%, 40%, and 20%) [S2].

drawbacks.text: As written, the payroll tax on earnings above the wage cap phases all the way down to zero for 2029 and every year after, while the bill permanently counts those above-cap earnings toward benefits. After 2029, high earners would gain benefit credit from income the system no longer taxes, leaving the higher investment-income tax as the main revenue source.

The bill substantially increases benefits permanently while its revenue side was never scored by the Congressional Budget Office and never examined in a hearing, so whether it actually improves Social Security's long-term finances is untested.

The 3-point increase in the investment income tax falls on capital gains, dividends, and passive income above $200,000 for single filers, which critics argue discourages investment; the transitional above-cap payroll tax would also hit high-earning professionals and small-business owners directly.

Caregiver credits require applications, physician documentation for chronically dependent relatives, and periodic recertification, which adds paperwork that could deter some eligible caregivers from claiming the credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit gains are real and targeted: they lift the floor for the poorest retirees, help the oldest beneficiaries, and reward care work the current formula ignores. The taxes fall almost entirely on the top of the income distribution. The design weakness is on the financing side — the above-cap payroll tax disappears after 2028 while above-cap earnings keep counting toward benefits, so the permanent revenue rests on the single investment-income tax increase, and the bill was never scored or debated, leaving its long-term arithmetic unverified.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, got no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the bill on September 11, 2024, near the end of the 118th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households and investors are better off because the bill died: no new tax on investment income and no payroll tax above the wage cap. Social Security beneficiaries, especially low earners and the oldest retirees, are no better off, and the program's long-term financing gap remains unaddressed.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no colleague joined him.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the roughly four months before the Congress expired.

against.name: The other 99 senators
against.what_they_did: Not one senator signed on as a cosponsor, including none from the Republican majority or from Schatz's own party.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the only measurable signal is that a single Democrat sponsored the bill and zero senators of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill raises the net investment income tax on capital gains and other investment income from 3.8% to 6.8%, with 44.1% of the revenue directed to the Social Security trust fund. Because the bill died, no new tax was imposed.

For 2025 through 2028 the bill applies Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above the annual cap, phasing down each year. These earners would have paid Social Security tax on income that is currently exempt above roughly $168,000.
